## Slide 2 — "Hengel (2022) showed readability differs — we ask: what else?"

**Content:** Two-column contrast layout. Left column describes the Hengel (2022) finding; right column states this paper's extension.

### Left column — Hengel (2022)

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Female-authored papers are more readable" | Paper p. 2: "Hengel 2022, who shows that female-authored papers are more readable" |
| "The gap widens during peer review" | Paper p. 2: "the writing gap widens during peer review" |
| "consistent with higher writing standards" | Paper p. 2: "consistent with women facing higher writing standards in publication" |
| "One dimension measured: Flesch Reading Ease" | Paper p. 2: "Flesch Reading Ease"; Table 1 (p. 10) shows Flesch as the first of five traditional readability measures Hengel computed |

### Right column — This paper

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Is readability the whole story?" | Paper p. 2: "We extend that insight beyond readability by measuring a broader set of surface-level writing features" |
| "We measure 15 additional surface features" | Paper Section 3.1 (p. 6): the rubric covers 16 criteria total; readability is one; the other 15 are listed in Table 2 (p. 14) |
| Examples listed (directness, jargon, novelty claims, assertiveness, hedging, evidence, emotional valence) | Paper p. 2: "directness, jargon, evidence and citation usage, active voice, novelty claims, hedging, and related rhetorical dimensions"; Table 2 (p. 14) |
| "9,117 abstracts" | Paper Section 4.1 (p. 7): "we have 9117 articles"; Table 4 (p. 15) gives the breakdown by journal and decade |
| "16-item LLM rubric" | Paper Section 3.1 (p. 6): "We use a 16-item rubric"; Table 2 (p. 14) lists all 16 criteria |

## Slide 5 — "Female-majority teams score higher on clarity, not on tone or emotion"

**Content:** Full-slide horizontal bar chart (Figure B from `generate_slide_figures.py`). Sixteen standardized criteria ranked by the female-minus-male mean difference, with 95% confidence intervals. Positive values indicate female-majority teams score higher; the Jargon bar is sign-flipped so positive = less jargon. A dashed horizontal line separates the top eight (clarity and related) from the bottom eight (tone and affect).

### Figure (fig_mean_differences.pdf)

The figure reproduces the key information from Figure 2 (p. 11) of the paper.

| Element | Source |
|---------|--------|
| Female–male mean difference across all 16 standardized criteria | Figure 2 (p. 11); Figure 2 caption: "Figure shows differences in means with 95% confidence intervals across the 16 criteria" |
| Classification: female if ≥50% of authors are female | Figure 2 caption (p. 11): "Papers are classified as female if at least 50% of authors are female, and male otherwise"; paper Section 5.2 (p. 9): "if at least 50% are female we call it female and male otherwise" |
| All criteria standardized (mean zero, unit SD) | Figure 2 caption (p. 11): "All criteria are standardized (mean zero, unit standard deviation) for comparability" |
| Jargon sign-flipped | Figure 2 caption (p. 11): "The sign of 'Jargon Technical Density' is reversed so that positive values indicate less jargon for female-majority papers" |
| Approximate bar magnitudes (Readability ~0.55, Jargon ~0.48, Active voice ~0.44, Pronoun ~0.40, Directness ~0.38, Evidence ~0.35) | Visually read from Figure 2 (p. 11); exact numerical values are not stated in the text but the Figure 2 bar chart is the authoritative source |
| Tone dimensions (assertiveness, hedging, qualifiers, modal, emotional valence, caution) near zero | Paper Section 5.2 (p. 11): "differences in tone — such as assertiveness, qualifiers, hedging, and emotional valence — are generally small or negligible" |

### Slide-title assertion

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "score higher on clarity, not on tone or emotion" | Paper Section 5.2 (p. 11): "Female-majority teams emphasize clarity – higher readability and greater directness – use more active voice, avoid jargon, and provide more evidentiary support through citations. In contrast, differences in tone — such as assertiveness, qualifiers, hedging, and emotional valence — are generally small or negligible" |

## Slide 6 — "The split is sharp: five clarity dimensions move, tone does not"

**Content:** Two-column layout with teal header ("Female > Male") and gray header ("Near zero"). The left column lists five dimensions with approximate standardized mean differences in SDs; the right column lists six tone/affect dimensions. This slide summarizes Figure 2 numerically for the audience.

> **Note on SD values:** The figures quoted (+0.55, +0.48, +0.44, +0.38, +0.35) are approximate visual reads from Figure 2 (p. 11). They are not numerically stated in the paper text; they are transcriptions of the bar heights in Figure 2. The regression coefficients for these same dimensions (controlled) are in Tables 11–12 (pp. 24–25) and are somewhat smaller.

### Left column — Female > Male

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Readability +0.55 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): largest bar; approximately 0.55 SD above male mean |
| Jargon (less) +0.48 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): second bar; Jargon/Technicality Density sign-flipped so positive = female teams use less jargon |
| Active voice +0.44 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): Active/Passive Voice Ratio bar |
| Directness +0.38 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): Sentence Length & Directness bar |
| Evidence +0.35 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): Evidence & Citation Usage bar |
| Novelty claims −0.05 SD | Figure 2 (p. 11): small negative bar; paper Section 5.2 (p. 11): "the exception of slightly weaker novelty claims...among female-majority teams" |

### Right column — Near zero

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Assertiveness near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24): −0.08 (SE 0.08), not significant |
| Hedging near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24): −0.21* (SE 0.11) — note this is marginally significant in col. 1 but small in magnitude |
| Qualifiers near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24): −0.02 (SE 0.10), not significant |
| Modal verbs near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24): −0.32* (SE 0.18) — marginally significant but close to zero in Figure 2 unconditional comparison |
| Emotional valence near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25): −0.02 (SE 0.02), not significant |
| Caution connectors near zero | Figure 2 (p. 11); Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24): 0.06 (SE 0.13), not significant |

> **Caveat for presenter:** Hedging (−0.21\*) and Modal Verb Strength (−0.32\*) are marginally statistically significant in the controlled regressions (col. 1 of Table 11, p. 24), though the unconditional differences shown in Figure 2 are small. The slide correctly characterizes them as near-zero in the *unconditional* comparison (Figure 2), but a discussant may raise that Hedging is −0.21\* in the OLS. The caption note "Unconditional; majority-gender classification" handles this.

### Caption

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Unconditional; majority-gender classification; all criteria standardized" | Figure 2 caption (p. 11) |

## Slide 7 — "Controls confirm five robust differences — tone dimensions are flat"

**Content:** Coefficient plot (`fig_regression_coefficients.pdf`). Each point is an OLS coefficient on `FemaleRatio` from a separate regression of that criterion on the full set of controls (col. 1 specification: journal×year FE, editor, blind, N_j). Horizontal lines are 95% confidence intervals. Teal = significant positive; dark red = significant negative; gray = not significant. A dashed line separates the five significant-positive dimensions (top) from the null/negative dimensions (bottom).

### Coefficient values (all from col. 1, full sample 1950–2015, N = 9,117)

| Criterion | Coefficient | SE | Significance | Source |
|-----------|-------------|-----|--------------|--------|
| Jargon (less dense) | +0.52 | 0.11 | *** | Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25) |
| Evidence & citation | +0.44 | 0.09 | *** | Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25) |
| Readability | +0.36 | 0.07 | *** | Table 1, col. 1 (p. 10); also Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25) |
| Directness | +0.27 | 0.10 | ** | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Ack. limitations | +0.23 | 0.12 | * | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Active voice | +0.07 | 0.10 | n.s. | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Hedging | −0.21 | 0.11 | * | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Assertiveness | −0.08 | 0.08 | n.s. | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Qualifier density | −0.02 | 0.10 | n.s. | Table 11, col. 1 (p. 24) |
| Emotional valence | −0.02 | 0.02 | n.s. | Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25) |
| Novelty claims | −0.32 | 0.10 | *** | Table 12, col. 1 (p. 25) |

### Controls (col. 1 specification)

| Control set | Source |
|-------------|--------|
| Editor fixed effects | Table 11/12 checkmarks (p. 24–25); Table 1 checkmarks (p. 10) |
| Blind-review indicator | Table 11/12 checkmarks (p. 24–25) |
| Journal×Year fixed effects | Table 11/12 checkmarks (p. 24–25), col. 1 uses journal×year |
| N_j (team size) | Not in col. 1; added in col. 2 and beyond (see Table 11/12 checkmarks) |

> **Note:** Col. 1 includes Editor ✓, Blind ✓, Journal×Year ✓ only — it does not include institution, quality, native speaker, or JEL controls, which are added in cols. 4–9. The text in the paper summarizes results for "columns 1 to 5" as confirming directness, jargon, evidence/citation, and readability as robust positive differences, and novelty as a significant negative difference (Section 5.3, p. 12).

### Slide-title assertion

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Controls confirm five robust differences" | Paper Section 5.3 (p. 12): "there are statistically significant positive (female higher) differences in Sentence length, technical jargon, Evidence/citation usage and readability, while there is significant negative (female lower) difference in novelty claims" |
| "tone dimensions are flat" | Paper Section 5.3 (p. 12), also Section 6 (p. 12): "differences in assertiveness, qualifiers, and emotional valence, show small or unstable differences" |

## Slide 8 — "The readability result holds across six authorship definitions"

**Content:** Bar chart (`fig_robustness.pdf`) with six grouped bars, one per authorship specification. Each bar is the OLS coefficient on the female authorship indicator from col. 1 of the corresponding robustness table, with 95% CIs.

### Coefficient values

| Specification | Coefficient | SE | Source |
|---------------|-------------|-----|--------|
| Female ratio (main) | 0.36*** | 0.07 | Table 1, col. 1 (p. 10), LLM Readability row |
| Majority female | 0.27*** | 0.05 | Table 6, col. 1 (p. 18), LLM Readability row |
| Any female author | 0.26*** | 0.05 | Table 7, col. 1 (p. 19), LLM Readability row |
| 100% female | 0.35*** | 0.08 | Table 8, col. 1 (p. 20), LLM Readability row |
| Solo female | 0.37*** | 0.10 | Table 9, col. 1 (p. 21), LLM Readability row |
| Senior female | 0.38*** | 0.08 | Table 10, col. 1 (p. 22), LLM Readability row |

### Definitions of each specification

| Specification | Definition | Source |
|---------------|------------|--------|
| Female ratio (main) | Continuous female-to-total author ratio (0 for strict male-majority) | Paper Section 3 (p. 5): "the gender variable is defined as the ratio of female to male authors" |
| Majority female | Binary: ≥50% female | Table 6 notes (p. 18): "dummy variable equal to 1 if a weak majority (50% or more) of authors are female" |
| Any female author | Binary: ≥1 female author | Table 7 notes (p. 19): "dummy variable equal to 1 if at least one author on a paper is female" |
| 100% female | Binary: all authors female | Table 8 notes (p. 20): "dummy variable equal to 1 if all authors on a paper are female" |
| Solo female | Binary: sole author is female (vs. sole author is male) | Table 9 notes (p. 21): "dummy variable equal to 1 if the paper is solo-authored by a woman and 0 if it is solo-authored by a man" |
| Senior female | Binary: senior female coauthor present (vs. all-male) | Table 10 notes (p. 22): "interaction between female ratio and a dummy variable equal to 1 if a female author had strictly more top-five papers as her co-authors" |

### Caption text

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "OLS coefficient on female authorship (col. 1 spec.)" | Tables 1, 6–10 (pp. 10, 18–22), col. 1 in each |
| "Pattern holds for jargon, directness, and evidence too" | Paper Section C.1 (p. 16): "These alternative specifications yield similar coefficients and statistically significant results for the LLM readability metric"; additional robustness tables for other criteria not shown in paper but noted in text |

## Slide 9 — "A skeptic would say: LLM scores may reflect model bias"

**Content:** Devil's advocate slide. Left column states the skeptical concern; right column gives the three-part response.

### The concern

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "GPT-5 may systematically rate female-associated writing as more readable regardless of actual linguistic content" | This is the standard critique of LLM-based measurement; acknowledged in the paper at Section 3.2 (p. 7): "there is still some randomness involved in the LLM evaluations. Because of this, the standard errors for analysis using LLM evaluations does not fully reflect the instability of our estimates" |

### Response (1) — Replication of Hengel's manually calculated scores

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "LLM readability replicates Hengel's manually calculated scores" | Figure 1 (p. 5) and Table 1 (p. 10); paper Section 5.1 (p. 9): "The validation exercise shows that the LLM readability measure tracks the same underlying pattern documented by Hengel 2022"; also paper p. 3: "The validation exercise shows that the LLM readability measure tracks the same underlying pattern" |

### Response (2) — Consistency across authorship specifications

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Consistent across six authorship specifications" | Tables 6–10 (pp. 18–22); paper Section C.1 (p. 16) and Section 5.1 (p. 9): "These alternative specifications yield similar coefficients and statistically significant results for the LLM readability metric, indicating robustness" |

### Response (3) — Null results for tone dimensions

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "A biased model would also flag assertiveness and hedging. It does not." | Figure 2 (p. 11): assertiveness, hedging, qualifiers, emotional valence bars are near zero; Tables 11–12 (pp. 24–25): assertiveness −0.08 (n.s.), emotional valence −0.02 (n.s.), qualifier density −0.02 (n.s.); paper conclusion (p. 12): "differences in assertiveness, qualifiers, and emotional valence, show small or unstable differences" |

## Slide 10 — Closing (dark background)

**Content:** Full-bleed dark navy slide. Large centered takeaway in white, with supporting detail below in light gray.

| Claim | Source |
|-------|--------|
| "Women in economics write more clearly." | Paper Section 6 (p. 12): "the most robust differences are not in emotionality or generalized lack of confidence. Instead, they are concentrated in clarity and presentation: female-majority teams write more readable and direct abstracts, use less jargon, generally provide more evidentiary support" |
| "Not more hesitantly. Not more emotionally." | Paper Section 6 (p. 12): "Other dimensions, such as assertiveness, qualifiers, and emotional valence, show small or unstable differences"; also abstract (p. 1): "differences in hedging, qualifiers, assertiveness, and emotional valence are small or inconsistent" |
| "The difference is in how ideas are packaged, not in how confidently they are held." | Paper Section 6 (p. 12): the paper "does not support a simple story in which women write in a uniformly more hesitant or emotional way. The clearest differences are concentrated instead in clarity, technical density, and the organization of claims" (Section 1, p. 3) |

## Backup Slide 1 — Empirical Specification

**Content:** The estimating equation and a two-column list of article-level and author-level controls.

| Element | Source |
|---------|--------|
| Equation: $R_j = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{FemaleRatio}_j + \gamma X_j + \delta Y_j + \varepsilon_j$ | Paper Section 4.2, Equation (1) (p. 8) |
| $X_j$: journal×year FE, editor controls, blind-review indicator, JEL codes, theory/empirical flag | Table 1 control checkmarks (p. 10); paper Section 4.2 (p. 8): "controlling for...journal, year, article, and author controls" |
| $Y_j$: institution FE, author prominence (max T FE), author seniority (max t FE), native-speaker indicator | Table 1 control checkmarks (p. 10): "Institution ✓, Quality ✓¹ [includes citation count, max. T fixed effects, max. t], Native speaker ✓" |
| "Nine specifications" | Table 1 (p. 10): nine columns (cols. 1–5 for 1950–2015, cols. 6–9 for 1990–2015) |
| "SEs clustered on editor" | Table 1 notes (p. 10): "Standard errors clustered on editor in parentheses" |
| Alternative authorship measures listed | Paper Section 3 (pp. 5–6); Tables 6–10 (pp. 18–22) |

| Figure file | Content | Paper source |
|-------------|---------|--------------|

| `fig_mean_differences.pdf` | Horizontal bar chart of 16 standardized female–male mean differences with 95% CIs | Figure 2 (p. 11); approximate bar heights read visually from Figure 2 |
| `fig_regression_coefficients.pdf` | Coefficient plot for 11 criteria with 95% CIs, significance color-coded | Tables 11–12, col. 1 (pp. 24–25) |
| `fig_robustness.pdf` | Six-bar chart of LLM readability coefficient across authorship specifications | Tables 1, 6–10, col. 1 (pp. 10, 18–22) |
